notes: Adversarial regression suite. Each eval plants one trap from the Where Mistakes Hide table in its facts and is graded on its Must and Must not lines; Should lines are advisory. Every quantity the arithmetic depends on is defined in the prompt, no Must depends on a [VERIFY] fact, outcome labels are the skill's own (Available, Available with conditions, Not available; Qualifies, Fails, Uncertain), and each expected_output names the Checkpoint A hard stops checked. Figures were recomputed by an independent script on October 30, 2026 and rechecked on October 31, 2026. Each Must line states one requirement. Eval 1: deemed sale tax T = 0.21 x (600 + 100 + T - 220) converges by iteration and closed form to 127.5949; ADSP and AGUB 827.595; step-up 607.595; annual amortization 40.506; annual saving 8.506; 15-year annuity factor at 8% 8.55948; PV 72.810; net cost 54.785; 338(g) deadline Tuesday, June 15, 2027, not moved by IRC 7503. Eval 2: pre-signing date Friday, February 27, 2026 (signing Monday, March 2, 2026); 2,000,000 x $10 = $20.0m stock and $80.0m cash, 20.0%; 50.0% at $40. Eval 3: gross profit 95% for each founder; Ben 2026 gain 22.8 and basis recovered 1.2; Ana 33.0 (compensation reading) or 34.2 (purchase price reading); user plan 48.0 and 32.0 (total 80.0 against 55.8 or 57.0, an overstatement of 24.2 or 23.0). Eval 4: residual allocation I 5, III 20, IV 30, V 60, VI 50, VII 35; buyer 2026 deductions 62.833 against 91.833 under its draft (overstatement 29.0); seller 1245 recapture 45.0 against 5.0 under its draft. Eval 5: closing at the end of Tuesday, June 30, 2026; 181 days January 1 to June 30, 2026; property tax 0.9m x 181/365 = 446,301.37; State X closing of the books 240,000.00 against per diem 595,068.49 (difference 355,068.49). Eval 4 depends on 100 percent bonus depreciation for property acquired after January 19, 2025 under Pub. L. 119-21 as in force on the check date; re-check if the law changes.

evals.name: 338h10-proposed-for-fund-owned-c-corporation
evals.prompt: We are Osprey Industries Inc., a Delaware C corporation that files a consolidated federal return. On August 14, 2026 we signed a stock purchase agreement to buy 100% of the stock of Kestrel Instruments Inc. for $600.0m cash (the price paid for the stock), closing September 30, 2026. Kestrel is a Delaware C corporation that has never elected S status. Its stock is owned 85% by Larch Capital Fund IV, L.P. (a Delaware limited partnership taxed as a partnership) and 15% by four management individuals. Kestrel's aggregate adjusted tax basis in its assets is $220.0m, and it has $100.0m of liabilities (trade payables and accrued expenses, all of which would be taken into account in amount realized on a sale of its assets); it has no NOLs or credits. The seller's banker says we can make a joint 338(h)(10) election with Larch to get a step-up, and that if Larch won't sign we can make the 338(h)(10) election on our own. Tell us whether the 338(h)(10) works and, if not, whether any step-up election is worth it. Assumptions for this exercise: every Kestrel asset other than goodwill has fair market value equal to its tax basis, so all step-up is Class VII goodwill amortized under section 197; treat the amortization as 15 equal annual deductions, the first one year after closing; 21% federal rate; no state tax; 8% discount rate.
evals.expected_output: Labels 338(h)(10) and 336(e) Not available because the sellers are a partnership and individuals, says Osprey cannot make an (h)(10) election alone and that an invalid (h)(10) voids the 338 election, treats a unilateral 338(g) election as the only deemed asset route, solves its deemed sale tax to about $127.59m (ADSP and AGUB about $827.59m, step-up about $607.59m), and shows a goodwill tax shield worth about $72.81m, so the election costs about $54.78m net. Hard stops checked: the target's classification and owners are stated, the amount and form of consideration are stated, and no opinion-level, final-for-filing, back-dating or above-fair-value allocation is requested, so none fires.
expected_behavior: Must: label the 338(h)(10) election Not available.

Must: give as the reason that Kestrel's stock is sold by a partnership and individuals, not by a selling consolidated group, a selling affiliate or S corporation shareholders (Treas. Reg. 1.338(h)(10)-1(c)(1)).
Must: state that a 338(h)(10) election is made jointly with the sellers on Form 8023, so Osprey cannot make it alone (Treas. Reg. 1.338(h)(10)-1(c)(3)).
Must: state that if a 338(h)(10) election is not valid, the section 338 election is also not valid (Treas. Reg. 1.338(h)(10)-1(c)(5)).
Must: label a 336(e) election Not available because no seller is a domestic corporation and Kestrel is not an S corporation.
Must: identify a 338(g) election made by Osprey alone as the remaining deemed asset purchase route.
Must: state that under a 338(g) election Kestrel, owned by Osprey after closing, bears the deemed sale tax.
Must: state that under a 338(g) election the sellers are still taxed on their stock sale.
Must: solve the circular deemed sale tax to about $127.59m (21% of $600.0m + $100.0m + the tax - $220.0m).
Must: show a convergence or closed-form check of the deemed sale tax.
Must: report ADSP and AGUB of about $827.59m.
Must: report a step-up of about $607.59m.
Must: compute the present value of the goodwill tax saving as about $72.81m (about $8.51m a year for 15 years at 8%).
Must: compute the net cost of the 338(g) election as about $54.78m.
Must: state the 338(g) election deadline as Tuesday, June 15, 2027, the 15th day of the 9th month beginning after the September 2026 acquisition month, which IRC 7503 does not move.
Must not: present a joint or unilateral 338(h)(10) election as available for Kestrel.
evals.trap_note: Targets the trap-map row 'Cap table, entity documents and the seller's filing status'. A weak skill accepts the banker's premise (the prior version of this skill said only that the target must be an S corporation or a member of a consolidated or affiliated group) and never asks who the sellers are, or lets the buyer elect alone. The trap is live because Larch is a partnership and the other holders are individuals, so no eligible joint maker exists, and the only available route, 338(g), costs $127.59m now against a $72.81m present value of deductions.

evals.name: coi-measured-at-closing-instead-of-signing
evals.prompt: Please check our tax structure memo before it circulates internally. Harrow Corp. (publicly traded; one class of voting common stock) signed a merger agreement with Bellwood Systems, Inc. (a widely held Delaware C corporation whose shareholders are individuals and investment funds) on March 2, 2026; the agreement was binding on signing. Bellwood will merge with and into Harrow Merger Sub, Inc., a wholly owned Delaware corporate subsidiary of Harrow, with Merger Sub surviving and holding substantially all of Bellwood's assets; no Merger Sub stock is used. The merger consideration is fixed in the agreement: 2,000,000 Harrow voting common shares plus $80.0m in cash in total for all Bellwood shares, with no collar, price adjustment or election mechanism, and no Harrow shares will be redeemed. Harrow closed at $10.00 per share on February 27, 2026, the last business day before signing, and at $40.00 on October 29, 2026; closing is expected November 16, 2026. Harrow will continue Bellwood's business. The memo says the stock consideration is worth $80.0m of $160.0m (50%), so continuity of interest is satisfied and the merger qualifies as a forward triangular merger under 368(a)(2)(D), tax-free except for the cash. Is the memo right?
evals.expected_output: Applies the signing date rule to the fixed consideration, values the Harrow stock at $20.0m of $100.0m (20%) on February 27, 2026, labels COI Fails as in Treas. Reg. 1.368-1(e)(2)(v), Example 7, labels the 368(a)(2)(D) reorganization Fails, explains that a failed forward merger is a taxable transfer of Bellwood's assets followed by a liquidation with tax at the corporate and shareholder levels, and rejects the 50% closing-price measure. Hard stops checked: the target's classification and owners are stated, the amount and form of consideration are stated, and no opinion-level, final-for-filing, back-dating or above-fair-value allocation is requested, so none fires.
expected_behavior: Must: state that the agreement provides fixed consideration (a stated number of Harrow shares and amount of money) (Treas. Reg. 1.368-1(e)(2)(iii)).

Must: measure continuity of interest on Friday, February 27, 2026, the last business day before the contract became binding on Monday, March 2, 2026 (Treas. Reg. 1.368-1(e)(2)(i)), noting that this is a valuation date to which IRC 7503 does not apply.
Must: compute the stock consideration on that date as $20.0m (2,000,000 x $10.00), 20% of the $100.0m total.
Must: label continuity of interest Fails.
Must: cite the regulation's example in which stock worth 20% of the consideration does not preserve a substantial part of the proprietary interest (Treas. Reg. 1.368-1(e)(2)(v), Example 7).
Must: reject the memo's 50% figure because it uses the $40.00 price after signing.
Must: label the forward triangular merger under 368(a)(2)(D) Fails because it must qualify as if the merger were into Harrow, which requires continuity of interest.
Must: state that if the merger is not a reorganization, Bellwood is taxed at the corporate level on a taxable transfer of its assets.
Must: state that if the merger is not a reorganization, Bellwood's shareholders are taxed on all of their consideration, including the Harrow stock.
Must not: label the merger Qualifies.
Must not: describe the Harrow stock as received tax-free.
evals.trap_note: Targets the trap-map row 'Merger agreement consideration terms, signing date and pre-signing stock price'. A weak skill tests continuity at the closing price, sees 50% stock and passes the deal, or applies a remembered 40% threshold to the wrong date. The trap is live because the consideration is fixed, Harrow's price quadrupled after signing, and on the pre-signing date the boot is 80% of the value, the ratio the regulation's Example 7 holds does not preserve continuity.

evals.name: forfeitable-earnout-reported-as-fixed-price
evals.prompt: I'm preparing the founders' 2026 tax estimates. On August 31, 2026, Gannet Corp. bought 100% of the stock of Larkfield Analytics, Inc., a Delaware C corporation with one class of stock owned by two U.S. citizen individuals: Ana Ruiz, the CEO (60%, stock basis $3.0m), and Ben Cho, a co-founder who is not an employee (40%, stock basis $2.0m). The price is $60.0m cash at closing plus an earnout of up to $40.0m in total, payable in three annual installments in 2027, 2028 and 2029 based on revenue and split 60/40 between Ana and Ben. Under the stock purchase agreement, Ana's earnout share is forfeited if her employment with Gannet ends for any reason before a payment date; Ben's share is not tied to employment. Ana also signed a two-year employment agreement at her prior salary. An appraisal values the whole earnout at $25.0m at closing. Neither founder has decided whether to elect out of the installment method. My plan: report $85.0m of amount realized in 2026 (the $60.0m plus the $25.0m appraisal), all long-term capital gain, so Ana has $48.0m of gain and Ben $32.0m. For this exercise ignore imputed interest under sections 483 and 1274 (our adviser computes it separately) and ignore state tax. What should the 2026 figures be?
evals.expected_output: Explains that the earnout makes this a contingent payment sale reported on the installment method unless a founder elects out, computes Ben's 2026 gain at $22.8m (95% gross profit on $24.0m of cash), flags Ana's forfeitable earnout as at risk of compensation treatment and computes her 2026 gain as $33.0m under the compensation reading and $34.2m under the purchase price reading, and states that the $85.0m plan requires a timely election out and does not change the compensation question. Hard stops checked: the target's classification and owners are stated, the amount and form of consideration are stated, and no opinion-level, final-for-filing, back-dating or above-fair-value allocation is requested, so none fires.
expected_behavior: Must: state that a sale with payments after the year of sale whose total price cannot be fixed by year end is a contingent payment sale reported on the installment method unless the seller elects out (Treas. Reg. 15a.453-1(c)(1)).
Must: state that an election out must be made by the due date, including extensions, of the 2026 return (IRC 453(d)).
Must: compute Ben's stated maximum selling price as $40.0m ($24.0m cash plus his $16.0m maximum earnout).
Must: compute Ben's gross profit percentage as 95%.
Must: compute Ben's 2026 gain as $22.8m.
Must: compute Ben's 2026 basis recovery as $1.2m.
Must: flag Ana's earnout share as at risk of characterization as compensation because it is forfeited if her employment ends.
Must: compute Ana's 2026 gain under the compensation reading as $33.0m on her $36.0m of cash.
Must: state that under the compensation reading Ana's earnout of up to $24.0m is ordinary compensation income when paid.
Must: compute Ana's 2026 gain under the purchase price reading as $34.2m (a $60.0m stated maximum selling price and 95% gross profit).
Must: state that under the compensation reading the payer deducts Ana's payments when paid rather than adding them to Gannet's stock basis.
Must: state that reporting the $25.0m appraised value as 2026 amount realized requires a timely election out of the installment method.
Must: state that under an election out the contingent obligation is included at fair market value (Treas. Reg. 15a.453-1(d)(2)(iii)).
Must: state that an election out does not change the compensation analysis of Ana's share.
Should: route wage withholding on Ana's payments under the compensation reading to analyzing-compensation-tax.

Should: flag the section 453A interest charge for an installment obligation from a sale price over $150,000 and mark the measurement of a contingent obligation's face amount for the $5,000,000 threshold [VERIFY].

Should: note that Larkfield appears to meet the 280G small business corporation exemption (one class of stock, two U.S. citizen individual shareholders) if it is not an ineligible corporation under section 1361(b)(2).
Must not: present $48.0m and $32.0m of 2026 gain as the default result.
Must not: report Ana's forfeitable earnout as capital gain without the compensation reading.
evals.trap_note: Targets the trap-map row 'Earnout, escrow, holdback and seller note terms'. A weak skill books the appraised earnout as fixed 2026 consideration and calls it all capital gain, because it never applies the installment default for contingent payment sales and never reads the forfeiture term. The trap is live because the earnout is contingent and payable over 2027-2029, the user's plan overstates 2026 gain by $23.0m to $24.2m ($80.0m against $57.0m or $55.8m), and Ana's share is forfeited on termination of employment, the strongest compensation indicator.

evals.name: allocation-out-of-order-and-inconsistent-8594
evals.prompt: I head tax at Crestline Holdings Inc., a Delaware C corporation on a calendar year. Under an asset purchase agreement signed May 12, 2026, we bought the operating assets of Harlow Fabrication LLC (taxed as a partnership and owned by two individuals unrelated to Crestline) for $200.0m cash, closing July 1, 2026; we assumed no liabilities. The signed appraisal values the assets at closing as: cash $5.0m; accounts receivable $20.0m; inventory $30.0m; machinery and equipment $60.0m (all 7-year MACRS property Crestline never used before); customer relationships $35.0m; trade name $15.0m. Harlow's adjusted basis in the machinery is $15.0m (original cost $70.0m, depreciation taken $55.0m). APA section 2.7 says only that the parties 'will cooperate on an allocation'. Our draft allocation, in $m: cash 5, receivables 20, inventory 30, machinery 90, customer relationships and trade name 50, goodwill 5, because machinery gets 100% bonus depreciation. Harlow's draft: cash 5, receivables 20, inventory 30, machinery 20, customer relationships and trade name 30, goodwill 95. Which allocation is right, what goes on Form 8594, and what are our 2026 deductions from the purchase? Treat section 197 amortization as monthly from July 2026.
evals.expected_output: Allocates by the residual method (Class I $5.0m, III $20.0m, IV $30.0m, V $60.0m, VI $50.0m, VII $35.0m), rejects Crestline's draft because Class V exceeds fair market value and Harlow's because it takes the residual before Classes V and VI reach fair market value, computes Crestline's 2026 deductions of about $62.83m against $91.83m under its draft, shows Harlow's section 1245 recapture of $45.0m against $5.0m under its draft, and recommends an agreed binding schedule and matching Forms 8594. Hard stops checked: the target's classification and owners are stated, the amount and form of consideration are stated, and no opinion-level, final-for-filing, back-dating or above-fair-value allocation is requested, so none fires. The user asks which allocation is right rather than asking to file an above-fair-value allocation.
expected_behavior: Must: allocate by class in order with fair market value caps: Class I $5.0m, Class III $20.0m, Class IV $30.0m, Class V $60.0m, Class VI $50.0m, and the $35.0m residual to Class VII, totaling $200.0m.

Must: state that Crestline's draft allocates $90.0m to Class V, above its $60.0m fair market value, which the residual method does not permit (Treas. Reg. 1.338-6(c)(1), applied by Treas. Reg. 1.1060-1(c)).
Must: state that Harlow's draft puts $95.0m in Class VII while Classes V and VI receive less than fair market value, so it allocates out of class order.
Must: compute $60.0m of 100% bonus depreciation on the machinery, because it was acquired after January 19, 2025, by purchase from an unrelated seller, and not previously used by Crestline.
Must: compute about $2.83m of 2026 section 197 amortization ($85.0m over 180 months, for 6 months).
Must: compare Crestline's 2026 deductions of about $62.83m under the correct allocation with about $91.83m under its draft.
Must: show Harlow's section 1245 recapture on the machinery as $45.0m under the correct allocation against $5.0m under Harlow's draft.
Must: state that Crestline and Harlow each file Form 8594 with the return for the year that includes the sale date.
Must: state that a written allocation agreement binds both parties under section 1060(a).
Must: recommend an agreed allocation schedule before either party files.
Must: hand the allocation clause to asset-purchase-agreement.
Must not: endorse either draft allocation for Form 8594.
evals.trap_note: Targets the trap-map row 'Allocation schedule, appraisal and Form 8594 drafts'. A weak skill picks one party's draft, or averages them, because it does not apply the class order and the fair market value cap, and it misses that inconsistent Forms 8594 are a problem. The trap is live because both drafts sum to $200.0m and look plausible, yet the buyer's overstates its 2026 deductions by $29.0m and the seller's understates its ordinary recapture by $40.0m.

evals.name: tax-indemnity-misses-consolidated-liability-and-straddle
evals.prompt: We represent Atlas Freight Holdings, Inc., a Delaware C corporation that is not part of the seller's group, in buying 100% of the stock of Pinecrest Logistics, Inc. from Seller Parent Corp. for $150.0m cash, closing at the end of the day on June 30, 2026. Pinecrest is a C corporation and has been a member of Seller Parent's calendar-year consolidated federal return group since 2015. No 338(h)(10) or 336(e) election will be made. Draft SPA section 9.1 has Seller indemnify Atlas for 'Taxes of the Company for any taxable period ending on or before the Closing Date'; the draft has no straddle-period definition. Disclosure Schedule 3.15(b) lists an open IRS examination of Seller Parent's consolidated returns for 2022 and 2023 with a proposed adjustment of $3.0m attributable to another Seller Parent subsidiary. Pinecrest also files a separate calendar-year State X corporate income tax return (State X has no combined reporting) at a 6% rate: its State X taxable income is $4.0m for January 1 through June 30, 2026 on a closing of the books, and is projected at $20.0m for the full 2026 year. Pinecrest owes $0.9m of real property tax for calendar 2026. Our corporate team will draft the clause; give us the tax analysis they need.
evals.expected_output: Identifies Pinecrest's several liability under Treas. Reg. 1.1502-6 for Seller Parent's consolidated tax, including the disclosed $3.0m proposed adjustment, which the 'Taxes of the Company' wording does not clearly reach; explains that Pinecrest's federal year ends at the end of June 30, 2026 with pre-closing income on the seller group's return; computes the State X straddle split ($240,000 on a closing of the books against about $595,068 per diem) and the property tax split (about $446,301 per diem); and hands the analysis to stock-purchase-agreement, disclosure-schedules and managing-tax-controversy. Hard stops checked: the target's classification and owners are stated, the amount and form of consideration are stated, and no opinion-level, final-for-filing, back-dating or above-fair-value allocation is requested, so none fires.
expected_behavior: Must: state that under Treas. Reg. 1.1502-6 Pinecrest is severally liable for the entire consolidated federal income tax of Seller Parent's group for each year it was a member.
Must: state that this several liability includes the $3.0m proposed adjustment attributable to another subsidiary.
Must: state that indemnified taxes defined as 'Taxes of the Company' for pre-closing periods do not clearly reach that liability.
Must: state that the definition should expressly cover 1.1502-6 liability and similar state, local or foreign liability.
Must: treat the disclosed examination as a Pinecrest liability for indemnity purposes.

Must: state that Pinecrest's federal taxable year ends at the end of Tuesday, June 30, 2026 and its pre-closing income is reported on Seller Parent's consolidated return (Treas. Reg. 1.1502-76(b)(1)(ii)(A)).
Must: state that there is therefore no federal income tax straddle period.
Must: mention the next day rule for closing-day transactions after the closing (Treas. Reg. 1.1502-76(b)(1)(ii)(B)).
Must: compute State X income tax for the pre-closing period as $240,000 on a closing of the books.
Must: compute State X income tax for the pre-closing period as about $595,068 per diem (181 of 365 days of the $1.2m full-year tax).
Must: compute the pre-closing share of the 2026 real property tax as about $446,301 per diem (181 of 365 days of $0.9m).
Must: treat the straddle convention as a policy election for the parties.
Must: hand the drafting of the tax indemnity and straddle definitions, with these figures, to stock-purchase-agreement.
Must: hand the scheduling of the disclosed examination to disclosure-schedules.
Must: hand the defense of the examination to managing-tax-controversy.
Should: recommend a special indemnity or escrow for the disclosed examination.
Should: tie indemnity survival to the statute of limitations, with state limitation periods marked [VERIFY].
Must not: describe draft section 9.1 as covering the disclosed examination without changes.
Must not: describe draft section 9.1 as covering the State X and property tax straddle periods without changes.
evals.trap_note: Targets the trap-map row 'Tax representations, tax indemnity and tax covenants in the draft agreement', which is also the party and scope row for whose tax the indemnity reaches. A weak skill reads 'Taxes of the Company' as complete, treats the disclosed examination as Seller Parent's problem, and allocates the state and property taxes without a straddle rule. The trap is live because the $3.0m adjustment belongs to another group member yet binds Pinecrest under 1.1502-6, and the State X convention choice moves about $355,068 between the parties.
